channel.title: Universe Today
channel.description: Space and Astronomy News from Universe Today

item.title: Asymmetric space waves map pressure on Earth's magnetic shield
item.dc:creator: Laurence Tognetti, MSc
item.author: Laurence Tognetti, MSc (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/laurencetognetti)
item.description: The Earth’s magnetic field is responsible for shielding us from harmful space weather, including solar radiation from the Sun but also cosmic rays originating from outside our solar system. Cosmic rays can include deep space supernovas, so the magnetic field takes the majority of the brunt from solar radiation. Without our magnetic field, the solar wind would slowly strip away our atmosphere, making life on our small, blue world impossible to exist. But where is the magnetic field doing the heaviest lifting regarding how it filters out incoming space radiation?

item.title: A Brief-ish History of METI. Part I: Early Ideas and Experiments
item.dc:creator: Matthew Williams
item.author: Matthew Williams (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/houseofwilliams)
item.description: For as long as scientists have conducted SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) experiments, parallel efforts in Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI) have also been mounted. In this series, we'll take a look at the major milestones in this field of study.

item.title: A Huge and Powerful New Simulation Helps Explain the Universe's Reionization
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: Cosmologists have another powerful simulation to work with. Lumina is the one of the largest and most detailed cosmological simulations yet and runs on the Frontier supercomputer. It's larger and more detailed than Illustris TNG.

item.title: Scientists Can Now Spot Hidden Sunspots on the Solar Far Side
item.dc:creator: Andy Tomaswick
item.author: Andy Tomaswick (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/andy-tomaswick)
item.description: Unlike the Moon, the Sun is constantly rotating from our perspective - but we still only see half of it at any given time. Since it takes 27 days to complete a full rotation, that leaves plenty of time for changes to happen to the side we can’t see that could directly impact Earth’s own space weather a few weeks later. Now a team of physicists led by Bibhuti Kumar Jha of the Southwest Research Institute has published a paper in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series that uses probability to map out what might be happening on the far side of the Sun, even if we can’t see it directly.

item.title: Parker Solar Probe Spots Twisted Magnetic Braids Growing in the Solar Wind
item.dc:creator: Andy Tomaswick
item.author: Andy Tomaswick (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/andy-tomaswick)
item.description: The magnetic environment around the Sun is a jumbled mess of chaotic fields and streams of charged particles. Recently we’ve been getting at least slightly better at mapping out its complexity, thanks in large part to data collected by missions like the Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter. But there’s still a large grey area surrounding the interface between the large scale hydrodynamic properties of plasmas and the microscopic properties of individual ions, and scientists believe understanding large scale features of the Sun, such as why its corona is so much hotter than its surface, may rely on our knowledge of that interface. A new paper that directly tackles some of the outstanding questions about that interface was recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by Masatomi Iizawa of the Technical University of Braunschweig and his co-authors.

item.title: A Merger Solves a Puzzling Paradox in Orion
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: Some of the Hubble Space Telescope's earliest observations were of the Orion Nebula. Those images showed proplyds, and subsequent observations uncovered a paradox centered on them. Given their rate of mass loss, those disks should have been destroyed long ago. Why weren't they?

item.title: Rare Lunar Meteorites Could Fill Gaps In Moon’s Evolution
item.dc:creator: Bruce Dorminey
item.author: Bruce Dorminey (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/bruce)
item.description: Almost all meteorites come from asteroids, not the Moon or Mars. But after decades of analysis of the Apollo samples, researchers still rely on lunar meteorites to better understand our anomalously large Moon.

item.title: White Dwarfs Are Actually…Yellow, Green, Pink, and Purple?
item.dc:creator: Laurence Tognetti, MSc
item.author: Laurence Tognetti, MSc (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/laurencetognetti)
item.description: The universe hosts a myriad of star types, including supergiants, giants, main sequence, red dwarfs, brown dwarfs, white dwarfs, and neutron stars. What makes these stars stand out are just their sizes, but their colors, as each one hosts a distinct color based on their surface temperature, specifically orange, red, blue, and white based on cooler to hotter temperatures. While the correlation between star colors and surface temperatures has long been known throughout astronomy, what if star colors could change based on specific criteria, including their atmosphere?

item.title: 27 Exoplanet Targets for the World's First Private Space Telescope
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: Get ready for the age of private space telescopes. The Lazuli Space Telescope will launch in a few years and part of its mission is to observe exoplanets. New research presents a list of 27 exoplanet targets, some of which are very well-known and will certainly benefit from deeper observations.

item.title: The Largest Canyon in the Solar System is Still Tectonically Active
item.dc:creator: Matthew Williams
item.author: Matthew Williams (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/houseofwilliams)
item.description: Scientists at Imperial College London and Columbia University have found that the largest canyon system in the solar system is still active and shaping Mars today, billions of years after it first formed.

item.title: Saudi Arabia Joins the Search for Alien Civilizations
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: Saudi Arabia is joining the search for alien signals coming from the cosmos. They're collaborating with SETI in the endeavour. SETI has announced that two LaserSETI instruments will be positioned in Saudi Arabia, adding to a growing network of optical sensors designed to detect laser pulses that could come from alien technological civilizations.

item.title: Magnetic Field Reversals and Extinctions: The Correlation Won't Go Away.
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: Scientists have wondered about a connection between Earth's geomagnetic reversals, or pole flips, and mass extinctions. They've found correlations, but nothing convincing enough to remove healthy doubts. But new research found a period of time with a concentrated number of reversals that coincides with and extinction and Large Igneous Provinces. It's likely not definitive proof, but it's certainly intriguing.

item.title: JWST Reveals a Lopsided Alien World with Blistering Evening Winds
item.dc:creator: Andy Tomaswick
item.author: Andy Tomaswick (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/andy-tomaswick)
item.description: Typically, when we think of exoplanets, we think of neat spheres floating directly in front of their star, which acts as a giant spotlight. From our vantage point, they would look more like two perfect two dimensional circles than spheres, though. But nature is almost never so clean-cut. A new paper published in Nature Astronomy from researchers at Cornell and the University of Bristol details the first-ever study of an exoplanet that is noticeably lopsided.

item.title: Advancing Astronomy at MIT with X-ray Reverberation Mapping
item.dc:creator: Matthew Williams
item.author: Matthew Williams (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/houseofwilliams)
item.description: Professor Erin Kara of MIT's Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research is helping advance our understanding of the most extreme objects in the Universe by analyzing X-ray reverberations and other astrophysical data.

item.title: Even the Rubin's Test Camera Produces Stunning Images
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: The Vera Rubin Observatory's Commissioning Camera operated for about 7 weeks in 2024, before the observatory released its well-known first look images. It's an engineering camera, and its job was to test the VRO's equipment and procedures. Now, the VRO has released the ComCam's image of the Seagull nebula. It's a pretty stunning image for an engineering camera.

item.title: Two Disks in One: How Accretion Disks Drive Black Hole Jets
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: SMBH jets are driven by thick, hot accretion disks with powerful magnetic fields. But there's a bit of a paradox. Some SMBH produce jets, even though they appear to have thin, cold accretion disks. New research has solved this paradox, showing that disks can be truncated into an outer cold disk and an inner hot disk.

item.title: New Evidence for an Old Prediction: Recoiling Supermassive Black Holes
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: Theory says that during some SMBH mergers, the merger remnant receives a recoil kick from gravitational waves. Instead of sitting placidly in the galactic center, these recoiled SMBH are sent on a pendulum-like motion, back and forth through the galactic center. New research has found statistical evidence supporting their existence.

item.title: From Dusk, Towards Dawn: Venus Slides Past the Sun This Weekend
item.dc:creator: David Dickinson
item.author: David Dickinson (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/david-dickinson)
item.description: Where have all the planets gone? Late October 2026 sees a decided dearth of planets in the dusk sky, with only bashful Mercury receding from view, and Saturn fresh off of opposition. Venus, the former lucida of the evening sky is now lost from view, taking the plunge sunward. But this vanishing act allows for a dramatic transformation this weekend, as our nearest planetary neighbor brushes past the Sun and transitions into the dawn sky.

item.title: Autonomous Triangular Modules Could Build Tomorrow’s Mega-Observatories
item.dc:creator: Andy Tomaswick
item.author: Andy Tomaswick (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/andy-tomaswick)
item.description: Private companies are getting better and better at launching more and more mass into space with larger and larger rockets. But, there is still a major constraint on the size of objects we can get into orbit - fairing size. This places physical constraints on the overall shape of what we can launch, and severely limits the sizes of, say, a communications array or a power satellite. But a new paper from researchers at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and the Beijing Institute of Technology offers a solution - a self-shaping, deployable module that can fine-tune both its positioning and its own dimensions.

item.title: Supernova Explosions First Aided, Then Later Impeded, the Epoch of Reionization
item.dc:creator: Evan Gough
item.author: Evan Gough (https://www.universetoday.com/authors/ion23drive)
item.description: The Epoch of Reionization is when radiation from early galaxies and their stars reionized neutral hydrogen and let light travel freely through the cosmos. Some research shows that supernovae helped the process. But new research shows that, though they may have helped initially, supernovae eventually slowed reionization.
